bib.title: AI Chains: Transparent and Controllable Human-AI Interaction by Chaining Large Language Model Prompts
bib.venue: CHI '22, April 29-May 5, 2022, New Orleans, LA, USA

read.skipped: Reference list skimmed for lineage only.

question: Can chaining several narrowly scoped LLM prompts, with the intermediate data visible and editable, make an LLM more transparent, controllable and effective on complex tasks than a single prompt?
hypothesis: Decomposing a problem into smaller, highly targeted tasks is likely to increase model performance on those sub-tasks, and by extension, the overarching task.
contributions: We introduce the notion of LLM Chaining: a series of chained model calls, each targeting a small and well-scoped sub-task.
We design and implement building blocks for constructing and interacting with LLM Chains: a set of primitive LLM operations and an interactive interface showing intra- and inter-step structure.
We report results from a 20-person evaluation showing Chaining can increase system transparency, controllability, and task outcomes without changing the underlying model.

method.summary: The authors survey 73 online LLM demos to derive eight primitive operations (each with a prompt template, default temperature and data type), build an interface to compose them into Chains with editable intermediate data, and run a 20-person within-subject study against a single-prompt Sandbox interface using the same LaMDA 137B model. Two case studies (VegaLite bug fixing, assisted text entry) are shown qualitatively.
method.task: Human-LLM collaboration on multi-step writing tasks (peer review rewriting, flashcard creation) via prompt chaining; user study with Likert ratings, clickstream and paired outcome comparison

datasets.name: Survey of 73 online LLM demos
datasets.source: LLM official websites (GPT-3, Jurassic), social media, published case studies; links last accessed 2021/08 (Table 2)
datasets.preprocessing: Highly open-ended demos (e.g. generic chatbots) removed; remainder iteratively sorted into 8 primitives; refined with feedback from 3 pilot users.

datasets.name: VizLinter examples (VegaLite)
datasets.size: 10 cases (5 erroneous/fixed spec pairs as few-shot examples, 5 test cases)

other.training_data: more than 1.5T words of text data
other.note: Used for all Chain steps and the Sandbox baseline; the paper says the interface is model agnostic.

inference.temperature: Per-operation defaults: Classification 0.0, Information Extraction 0.2, Rewriting 0.3, Split Points 0.3, Compose Points 0.5, Factual Query 0.3, Generation 0.7, Ideation 0.7 (Table 3); users could change it via a knob in both interfaces.
inference.samples: Single run per click; users could re-run. Case study: 5 test cases, one Chain run each (not otherwise stated).
inference.prompting: Prompt template per operation: instruction (e.g. 'Given [prefix-1], the following is a list of [prefix-2].'), optional few-shot examples separated by '###', then input prefix and output prefix; output parsed to the operation's data type (string or numbered list).

parameters.operations: 8 primitives in 3 groups: validate/categorize (Classification), gather info (Factual Query, Generation, Ideation), re-organize (Information Extraction, Rewriting, Split Points, Compose Points)
parameters.data_mappings: Rewriting 1-1, Split Points and Ideation 1-N, Compose Points N-1

other.study_baseline_prompts: Sandbox users were given default prompts that were known to work reasonably (Appendix B.3-B.5).

metrics.name: Likert ratings (match goal, think through, transparent, controllable, collaborative)
metrics.definition: Seven-point scale, 1 strongly disagree to 7 strongly agree, asked once per interface

metrics.name: Consecutive runs
metrics.definition: Share of runs where the user changed nothing (or only formatting) after the previous run

metrics.name: Edit types (CURATE, UNDO, CREATE)
metrics.definition: How edits to text relate to existing model output, from logged clickstreams (Appendix B.2)

metrics.name: Paired outcome preference
metrics.definition: Two blinded non-participants chose which of a participant's Sandbox vs Chaining results best satisfied the task goals

baselines: Sandbox: a single-textbox interface based on the GPT-3 playground, same LaMDA model, adjustable temperature
eval.protocol: Within-subject, 20 participants, each performed one randomly selected task (Flashcard or Review) once per interface, order counterbalanced, up to 25 minutes per interface, 30-minute tutorial beforehand, ~90 minutes total, $40 gift certificate. Wilcoxon signed-rank for Likert, Student's t-test for clickstream shares and time. Qualitative thematic analysis by three researchers. Case studies judged by one author.

availability.data: A demo video is linked (https://youtu.be/QFS-1EWlvMM); no code or data release stated.

limits: Study uses only two predefined Chains and tasks (peer review, flashcards) that decompose naturally; participants used authored-by-researchers Chains, which the authors say may explain complexity complaints.
Tasks with interdependent sub-parts may lose coherence when split into independent sub-parts; dropping data layers may cause information loss (Sec 7).
Chaining limited free exploration; three participants preferred Sandbox for trying out random things.
Authoring of Chains by end users is left to future work (Sec 7).
Extra LLM calls add computational cost; the authors argue saved effort outweighs it but give no cost measurement.
Case studies are anecdotal: 5 test cases judged by one author, single-pass comparison not quantified.
No accuracy metric against ground truth on standard benchmarks; outcome quality comes from two raters' paired preference and self-ratings.
Eight primitives are not claimed to be exhaustive.
Used a non-dialog LaMDA 137B; models of 2021-22 era, instruction-tuned and chat models are not tested.
Decoding settings other than temperature, max tokens and seeds are not stated.

terms.definition: the process of breaking up complex tasks into smaller steps, where each step can be completed by an independent run of an LLM, and where the output of one or more steps is used as input for the next
the input data and output data of an LLM operation, which connect steps in a Chain

one of eight LLM sub-tasks (Classification, Factual Query, Generation, Ideation, Information Extraction, Rewriting, Split Points, Compose Points) well-scoped for a single model run, each with a default prompt template and temperature
errors or imperfections from previous runs can accumulate in autoregressive generation, so LLMs perform worse on long text and may repeat themselves
